newsitem.title: USA: Bond dealers oppose GFOA "yield burning" plan.
newsitem.headline: Bond dealers oppose GFOA "yield burning" plan.

text.p: Bond dealers told IRS on Thursday that many of them will not sell Treasury securities to state and local governments if they are required to disclose markups under a plan being pushed by municipalities.
"There are some people that would not bid," Arthur Miller, a vice president in the municipal bond department at Goldman Sachs & Co., warned Internal Revenue Service officials.
Miller was speaking on behalf of the Public Securities Association at a public hearing on IRS' rule proposal June 26 to curb yield burning in the muni market.

Under the proposed rule, localities that get three bona fide bids from dealers that have no material interest in the offerings would enjoy a "rebuttable presumption" that the securities were bought at fair market value.

The Government Finance Officers Association recommended recently that dealers certify to issuers that they sold them Treasuries at fair market value and that they disclose the price mark up in the certification.
GFOA offered the recommendation in a comment letter last week on IRS' yield burning rule.
GFOA said issuers that get three independent bids should enjoy a "safe harbor" from IRS liability instead of just a "rebuttable presumption."
But dealers today said that while they support a "safe harbor," they think the GFOA plan is unworkable.
"It is virtually unheard of that dealers would provide markup data," Michael Decker, vice president of policy analysis at the Public Securities Association, said.
"It would discourage government securities dealers from participating," Decker said.

Decker told Reuters that, currently, it is not unusual for issuers buying securities for escrow accounts in the municipal market to ask dealers to fill out bid forms and to return them with price information.
"That's not typical in government securities," however, he said.

"The notion of bid forms is quite alien to the Treasury market," Miller told IRS today. "Bids and offers are done over the phone" in government securities, he said. The more "burden" put on government dealers, the fewer the bidders, he added.
